title: Overview of hemostasis
covers: The phases and players of hemostasis, the endothelium, platelet receptors and vWF, the coagulation cascade and cell-based model, the natural brakes and fibrinolysis, bleeding patterns, and reading PT, aPTT and the other screening tests.

items.p: Hemostasis stops bleeding after injury without blocking the vessel. It is quick, localized, carefully regulated and balanced, and it happens in phases.

ul: Vasoconstriction of the damaged vessel
Primary hemostasis: the platelet plug
Secondary hemostasis: the fibrin clot
Tertiary hemostasis: fibrinolysis

items.p: It balances procoagulant and anticoagulant forces. Four main players: blood vessels, platelets, coagulation factors and the fibrinolytic system. Bleeding comes from a fragile vessel, too few or faulty platelets, a missing clotting factor, or a fibrinolysis defect.

table: Smooth surface: platelets do not stick
Nitric oxide and prostacyclin: dilate, inhibit platelets
Tissue factor exposed: starts the cascade
vWF released: glue between platelet and collagen
Thrombomodulin: switches thrombin to an anticoagulant role
TFPI: blocks the first step of the cascade

ul: Injury exposes subendothelial collagen → platelet adhesion
Platelets anchor through GPIb binding vWF
Activated GPIIb-IIIa binds fibrinogen and links platelets → aggregation
The plug appears in 3–5 minutes. It is soft and easily washed away, so a fibrin mesh must reinforce it.

table: Aggregation; the major platelet membrane protein

items.p: A large multimeric glycoprotein made by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes. ADAMTS-13 cleaves it to normal-sized multimers.

ul: Platelet adhesion: a bridge between platelets and the endothelium
Platelet aggregation
Fibrin clot formation: it carries factor VIII and cuts its clearance about 5-fold

items.p: Lecturer's note: von Willebrand disease is a mixed disorder. It affects primary (platelet) and secondary (factor VIII) hemostasis.

items.caption: Coagulation cascade with the lecturer's notes

ul: Intrinsic: XII → XI → IX; IXa with VIIIa activates X. Measured by the aPTT (plasma exposed to contact activators).
Extrinsic: tissue factor (III) with VIIa activates X. Measured by the PT (plasma exposed to tissue factor).
Common: Xa with Va turns prothrombin into thrombin; thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin; XIIIa cross-links it. The thrombin time measures fibrinogen → fibrin.

items.p: Lecturer's notes: a prolonged PTT with bleeding means factor VIII, IX or XI. The PT gives the INR. If the PT, aPTT, thrombin time and everything else are normal, think of factor XIII.
Secondary hemostasis is a series of interactions between factors on tissue factor-bearing cells and activated platelets.

table: VIIa/TF activates X and IX; a little thrombin
Thrombin activates platelets and cofactors (V, VIII freed from vWF, XI)
Tenase (IXa + VIIIa) and prothrombinase (Xa + Va) make a large thrombin burst

items.p: The fibrin clot forms in 5–10 minutes.

table: Substrate; low in liver disease and DIC
Vitamin K dependent; target of warfarin
Not in blood; exposed by injury
Removed by citrate in blood tubes
Shortest half-life; first to fall on warfarin
Cross-links fibrin; normal PT and aPTT

items.p: There is no factor VI: it turned out to be activated factor V.

items.note: Slide 12 says factor VIII is "not made in liver". Standard sources: VIII is made mainly by liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (not hepatocytes), so its level holds up in liver disease. Not tested as worded.

items.caption: Four brakes keep the clot at the injury

ul: Flow washes activated factors downstream; the liver clears them
TFPI blocks the TF–VII pathway and stops initiation
Antithrombin mops up thrombin and Xa
Protein C + protein S destroy Va and VIIIa
The intact wall carries thrombomodulin and heparan sulphate

items.p: If one brake fails, the patient clots: antithrombin, protein C or protein S deficiency, factor V Leiden.

Fibrinolysis: as the vessel heals, plasminogen activators turn plasminogen into plasmin inside the clot. Plasmin slowly dissolves fibrin into fibrin degradation (split) products. Deficiency of these regulators raises the risk of thrombosis.
Disorders are inherited or acquired: primary (platelet), secondary (factor), or mixed (both, e.g. vWD).

table: Petechiae, purpura, nosebleeds, heavy periods, gum bleeding

summary.h: History and exam in a bleeding child

ul: Bleeding: nose, gums, bruising, joints and muscles, heavy periods; neonatal bleeding; after dental extraction, surgery, circumcision or trauma; transfusions
Clues to other causes: pallor and infections; weight loss, night sweats, fever, lymphadenopathy, masses (malignancy); diet, drugs, travel
Family: consanguinity, bleeding relatives, hysterectomy at a young age. A negative family history does not exclude an inherited disorder.
Exam: general appearance and hemodynamics, fever, petechiae to hematomas, retinal hemorrhages, hemarthrosis and contractures, lymph nodes, liver and spleen, masses, bone deformities or absent bones

table: Warfarin, vitamin K deficiency, liver disease
XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, I
Hemophilia A or B, XI or XII deficiency, heparin, vWD, lupus anticoagulant
VII deficiency, early warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency, early liver disease
Liver disease, DIC, full warfarin, X, V, II or fibrinogen deficiency
Platelet disorder, vWD, vessel wall, factor XIII deficiency

items.p: Mixing study: mix the patient's plasma 1:1 with normal plasma. Correction = a missing factor; no correction = an inhibitor (antibody).

items.note: The platelet range here is 150–400 × 10⁹/L; the next lecture gives 150–450. Reference ranges vary by laboratory.

cards.a: Vasoconstriction → primary (platelet plug) → secondary (fibrin clot) → tertiary (fibrinolysis)
Blood vessels, platelets, coagulation factors, fibrinolytic system
Smooth surface; NO and prostacyclin; heparan sulphate (activates antithrombin); thrombomodulin; TFPI

cards.q: Injured endothelium: what is exposed or released?
cards.a: Collagen (platelets bind), tissue factor (starts cascade), vWF (glue); endothelin constricts
Adhesion: GPIb–vWF, GPIa-IIa–collagen. Aggregation: GPIIb-IIIa–fibrinogen.
Collagen receptor that promotes activation of GPIIb-IIIa and GPIa-IIa

cards.q: Platelet plug versus fibrin clot timing
cards.a: Plug 3–5 minutes; fibrin clot 5–10 minutes
Endothelial cells and megakaryocytes; ADAMTS-13 cleaves it to normal-sized multimers
Platelet adhesion (bridge), platelet aggregation, carries factor VIII (cuts its clearance 5-fold)

cards.q: Why is vWD a mixed disorder?
cards.a: It affects primary (platelet adhesion) and secondary (factor VIII) hemostasis

cards.q: PT versus aPTT: trigger and factors
cards.a: PT: tissue factor; VII, X, V, II, I. aPTT: contact activators; XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, I.

cards.q: Prolonged aPTT with bleeding: which factors?
cards.a: VIII, IX or XI

cards.q: Bleeding with normal PT, aPTT, thrombin time and platelets?
cards.a: Think factor XIII deficiency (fibrin not cross-linked)
Initiation (TF-bearing cell) → amplification (platelets and cofactors activated) → propagation (thrombin burst on platelets)

cards.q: Which factor falls first on warfarin, and why?
cards.a: Factor VII: shortest half-life (isolated PT prolongation early)

cards.q: Which factor is removed by citrate tubes?
cards.a: Factor IV (calcium)

cards.q: Why is there no factor VI?
cards.a: It was found to be activated factor V
Flow (liver clears factors), TFPI, antithrombin (thrombin, Xa), protein C + S (Va, VIIIa)
Plasminogen activators → plasmin → dissolves fibrin → fibrin degradation products
Primary: immediate, mucocutaneous, petechiae, small cuts bleed. Secondary: delayed, joints/muscles/deep, small cuts normal.
0.8–1.2 untreated; target usually 2–3
Heparin; low or abnormal fibrinogen
Factor VII deficiency, early warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency, early liver disease

cards.q: PT and aPTT both normal but bleeding: causes
cards.a: Platelet disorder, vWD, vessel wall disorder, factor XIII deficiency
Corrects = factor deficiency; does not correct = inhibitor (antibody)

questions.stem: Hemostasis stops bleeding after injury. What else defines a normal hemostatic response?

options.A: It seals the injury without blocking the vessel
options.B: It seals the vessel along its whole length
options.C: It acts through platelets without any fibrin
options.D: It activates coagulation throughout the blood
options.E: It replaces the vessel wall with fibrin

questions.explanation: Hemostasis is the process of stopping bleeding without blocking a vessel after injury. It is quick, localized, carefully regulated, balanced, and occurs in phases. B: The response is localized; the vessel stays open. C: The fibrin mesh is needed to reinforce the plug. D: Hemostasis is localized, not systemic. E: The clot is later dissolved as the vessel heals.

questions.stem: A vessel is cut. Which event comes first in hemostasis?
questions.explanation: Phases: vasoconstriction, then the platelet plug (primary), the fibrin clot (secondary), and fibrinolysis (tertiary). A: Primary hemostasis follows vasoconstriction. B: Secondary hemostasis. C: Propagation phase of secondary hemostasis. D: Tertiary hemostasis, last.

questions.stem: Which phase of hemostasis is called tertiary hemostasis?
questions.explanation: Primary = platelet plug; secondary = fibrin clot; tertiary = fibrinolysis. A: The first phase. B: Primary hemostasis. C: Secondary hemostasis. E: Final step of secondary hemostasis.

questions.stem: Besides blood vessels, platelets and coagulation factors, which is the fourth main player in hemostasis?
questions.explanation: Four main players: blood vessels, platelets, coagulation factors, fibrinolytic system. Bleeding can come from a fragile vessel, too few or faulty platelets, a missing clotting factor, or a defect in fibrinolysis. A: Not one of the four players. B: Not one of the four players. D: Not one of the four players. E: Not one of the four players.

questions.stem: A man with normal platelets and normal clotting factors bleeds easily. Which cause fits this picture?
questions.explanation: Bleeding can come from a fragile vessel, too few or faulty platelets, a missing clotting factor, or a defect in fibrinolysis. With normal platelets and factors, the vessel is the remaining player. A: His platelets are normal. C: His factors are normal. D: A platelet problem. E: A factor problem.

questions.stem: Which endothelial product dilates the vessel and inhibits platelets?
questions.explanation: Intact endothelium: smooth surface, nitric oxide and prostacyclin (dilate, inhibit platelets), heparan sulphate (activates antithrombin), thrombomodulin, TFPI. A: Constricts the injured vessel. B: Switches thrombin to an anticoagulant role. C: Starts the cascade. D: Glue between platelet and collagen.

questions.stem: How does heparan sulphate on intact endothelium prevent clotting?
questions.explanation: Heparan sulphate activates antithrombin, which blocks thrombin. A: Activated protein C does this. B: TFPI does this. D: Nitric oxide and prostacyclin. E: ADAMTS-13 does this.

questions.stem: Which endothelial molecule switches thrombin from a procoagulant to an anticoagulant role?
questions.explanation: Thrombomodulin on intact endothelium switches thrombin to an anticoagulant role. A: Activates antithrombin. C: Blocks the first step of the cascade. D: Dilates and inhibits platelets. E: Dilates and inhibits platelets.

questions.stem: Which endothelial inhibitor blocks the first step of the coagulation cascade?

options.C: Activated protein C with protein S

questions.explanation: TFPI blocks the TF–FVII pathway and stops initiation. B: Mops up thrombin and Xa. C: Destroys Va and VIIIa. D: Switches thrombin's role. E: Starts fibrinolysis.

questions.stem: Seconds after a vessel is injured, which endothelial product makes it constrict?
questions.explanation: Injured endothelium: collagen exposed, tissue factor exposed, vWF released, vessel constricts (endothelin), protective molecules lost. A: Dilates. B: Dilates. C: Anticoagulant. E: Anticoagulant.

questions.stem: At a site of vessel injury, which event starts the coagulation cascade?
questions.explanation: Injury exposes tissue factor, which starts the coagulation cascade; exposed collagen binds platelets. A: Primary hemostasis. C: Glue for platelet adhesion. D: Vasoconstriction. E: Loss of protection, not the trigger.

questions.stem: Platelets first anchor to an injured vessel through which interaction?
questions.explanation: Injury exposes subendothelial collagen; platelets anchor through GPIb binding vWF; activated GPIIb-IIIa binds fibrinogen and links platelets (aggregation). A: Aggregation, not anchoring. B: GPVI binds collagen. C: GPIa-IIa binds collagen. E: Not the anchoring step shown.

questions.stem: A patient's platelets stick normally to collagen but cannot bind fibrinogen. Which step of primary hemostasis fails?
questions.explanation: GPIIb-IIIa binds fibrinogen, linking platelets together: platelet aggregation. A: Adhesion to collagen is normal. B: Endothelin, not platelets. D: Factor XIIIa. E: Endothelial injury.

questions.stem: How long after injury does the platelet plug normally appear?
questions.explanation: The platelet plug appears in 3–5 minutes; the fibrin clot in 5–10 minutes. B: Too early. C: The fibrin clot. D: Too late. E: Too late.

questions.stem: Which platelet receptor binds collagen and promotes activation of GPIIb-IIIa?
questions.explanation: GPVI is a collagen receptor that promotes activation of GPIIb-IIIa and GPIa-IIa. A: vWF receptor, adhesion. B: Collagen receptor for adhesion. C: The fibrinogen receptor itself. D: Part of the vWF receptor complex.

questions.stem: Which receptor is the major platelet membrane protein?
questions.explanation: GPIIb-IIIa, the fibrinogen receptor that mediates aggregation, is the major platelet membrane protein. A: vWF receptor. C: Collagen receptor. D: Collagen receptor. E: Not the major membrane protein.

questions.stem: Platelet GPIa-IIa mediates which step?
questions.explanation: GPIa-IIa is a collagen receptor that mediates adhesion. A: GPIIb-IIIa. B: GPIb. C: Not a receptor role shown. D: GPVI activates GPIa-IIa, not the reverse.

questions.stem: Which cells make von Willebrand factor?
questions.explanation: vWF is a large multimeric glycoprotein made in endothelial cells and megakaryocytes. A: Not hepatocytes. B: Not macrophages. D: Not liver cells. E: Not fibroblasts.

questions.stem: A patient has no ADAMTS-13 activity. What accumulates in the plasma?
questions.explanation: ADAMTS-13 cleaves vWF to normal-sized multimers; without it, very large multimers persist. A: vWF carries factor VIII. B: Plasmin acts on fibrin. C: These come from ADAMTS-13 cleavage. E: Not the substrate of ADAMTS-13.

questions.stem: A man has very low von Willebrand factor. Why is his factor VIII level also low?

options.A: vWF normally slows factor VIII clearance
options.B: vWF is needed for factor VIII synthesis
options.C: vWF activates factor VIII on platelets
options.D: Factor VIII is used up in platelet plugs
options.E: Anti-vWF antibodies also bind factor VIII

questions.explanation: vWF carries factor VIII and decreases its plasma clearance about 5-fold. B: vWF carries VIII; it does not make it. C: Thrombin activates VIII. D: Not the mechanism. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Each is a function of von Willebrand factor EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: vWF promotes platelet adhesion (bridge), platelet aggregation, and fibrin clot formation by carrying factor VIII and decreasing its clearance. Thrombomodulin activates protein C. A: Adhesion. B: A vWF function. C: A vWF function. E: A vWF function.

questions.stem: Why is von Willebrand disease a mixed disorder of hemostasis?

options.A: It lowers both platelets and fibrinogen
options.B: It blocks both GPIIb-IIIa and GPVI
options.C: It affects platelet adhesion and factor VIII
options.D: It activates both plasmin and thrombin
options.E: It inhibits both ADAMTS-13 and protein C

questions.explanation: Lecturer's note: vWD is mixed; it affects primary (platelet) and secondary (factor VIII) hemostasis. A: Neither is the defect. B: Those are platelet receptors, not vWF. D: Not the mechanism. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Why is a platelet plug not enough to stop bleeding?

options.A: It forms after the fibrin clot
options.E: It is soft and easily washed away

questions.explanation: The platelet plug is soft and easily washed away; a fibrin mesh from the cascade reinforces it. A: The plug comes first. B: It persists until reinforced. C: Adhesion needs vWF, not fibrin. D: Hemostasis is localized.

questions.stem: Which factor starts the intrinsic pathway?
questions.explanation: Intrinsic pathway: XII → XI → IX (with VIIIa) → X. Extrinsic: TF + VIIa → X. Common: Xa + Va → thrombin → fibrin; XIIIa cross-links it. A: Extrinsic pathway. C: Activated by XIa. D: Common pathway. E: Cross-links fibrin.

questions.stem: A patient's factor deficiency prolongs the aPTT but leaves the PT normal. Which pathway is affected?
questions.explanation: Normal PT with prolonged aPTT points to the intrinsic pathway only (VIII, IX, XI, XII). B: Prolongs the PT. C: Prolongs both. D: Not measured by aPTT. E: Not measured by aPTT.

questions.stem: The PT measures how long plasma takes to clot after it is exposed to what?
questions.explanation: The PT measures time to clot when plasma is exposed to tissue factor; the aPTT when exposed to substances that activate contact factors. A: The aPTT. C: The thrombin time. D: Platelet aggregation testing. E: Platelet testing.

questions.stem: The aPTT is started by substances that activate which group of factors?
questions.explanation: The aPTT measures time for plasma to clot when exposed to substances that activate contact factors. A: Starts the PT. B: Not the trigger. C: Not part of the aPTT. E: Not part of the aPTT.

questions.stem: Which step does the thrombin time measure?
questions.explanation: Thrombin time: fibrinogen to fibrin conversion. A: Upstream of the test. B: Upstream of the test. C: Fibrinolysis. D: Factor XIII; not measured.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy has joint bleeds. His aPTT is prolonged and his PT is normal. A deficiency of which factor fits?
questions.explanation: Lecturer's note: a prolonged PTT with bleeding means factor VIII, IX or XI. Factor XI deficiency usually causes mild bleeding. B: Prolongs the PT. C: Normal PT and aPTT. D: Prolongs both. E: Prolongs both and the thrombin time.

questions.stem: A patient bleeds after surgery. His platelet count, PT, aPTT and thrombin time are normal, but his fibrin is not cross-linked. Which factor is deficient?
questions.explanation: Lecturer's note: if PT, aPTT, thrombin time and everything else are normal, think of factor XIII, which cross-links fibrin. A: Prolongs the aPTT. B: Prolongs the PT. D: Prolongs the thrombin time. E: Prolongs PT and aPTT.

questions.stem: In the cell-based model of coagulation, where does initiation occur?
questions.explanation: Initiation occurs on a TF-bearing cell; amplification activates platelets and cofactors; propagation generates large amounts of thrombin on the platelet surface. A: Propagation. B: Antithrombotic surface. C: Not in the model. E: The end product.

questions.stem: During propagation in the cell-based model, where is the large burst of thrombin made?

options.B: In free plasma away from cells
options.C: On activated platelets at the injury

questions.explanation: Propagation: large amounts of thrombin generated on the platelet surface at the injury site. A: Initiation; small amounts. B: Coagulation occurs on cell surfaces. D: Antithrombotic. E: Not in the model.

questions.stem: In the amplification phase, what does the first small amount of thrombin do?

options.B: Activates factor VII on the TF-bearing cell

questions.explanation: Amplification: platelets and cofactors (V, VIII released from vWF, XI) are activated, setting the stage for large-scale thrombin generation. A: That follows the thrombin burst. B: Initiation. C: Thrombomodulin does this on endothelium. D: XIIIa, at the end.

questions.stem: Which complex on the activated platelet activates factor X during propagation?
questions.explanation: Tenase (IXa + VIIIa) activates X on the platelet; prothrombinase (Xa + Va) makes the thrombin burst. A: Turns prothrombin into thrombin. C: Initiation, on the TF-bearing cell. D: Activates protein C. E: Inhibits thrombin.

questions.stem: After injury, about how long does the fibrin clot take to form?
questions.explanation: The fibrin clot occurs in 5–10 minutes; the platelet plug appears in 3–5 minutes. B: The platelet plug. C: Too early. D: Too late. E: Too late.

questions.stem: Blood for clotting tests is drawn into citrate tubes. Which factor does the citrate remove?
questions.explanation: Factor IV is calcium, used by both pathways and removed by citrate in blood tubes. A: Fibrinogen. B: Tissue factor, not in blood. C: Proaccelerin. E: Fibrin-stabilizing factor.

questions.stem: A patient starts warfarin. Two days later his PT is prolonged but his aPTT is still normal. What explains this?

options.A: Factor VII is not made in the liver
options.C: Factor IX is not vitamin K dependent
options.D: Heparin is needed to prolong the aPTT
options.E: Factor VII has the shortest half-life

questions.explanation: Factor VII has the shortest half-life and is the first to fall on warfarin, so early warfarin prolongs only the PT. A: It is a vitamin K-dependent liver factor. B: Warfarin blocks vitamin K-dependent synthesis. C: It is. D: Not the reason.

questions.stem: Proconvertin is the common name of which factor?
questions.explanation: V proaccelerin, VII proconvertin, VIII antihemophilic, IX Christmas, X Stuart–Prower, XI plasma thromboplastin antecedent, XIII fibrin-stabilizing. A: Proaccelerin. C: Stuart–Prower factor. D: Plasma thromboplastin antecedent. E: Christmas factor.

questions.stem: Which factor sits where the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways meet?
questions.explanation: Factor X (Stuart–Prower) is where the two pathways meet. A: Intrinsic. B: Extrinsic. D: Downstream, in the common pathway. E: Intrinsic.

questions.stem: Why is there no factor VI?

options.A: It was found to be activated factor V
options.B: It was found to be activated factor VII
options.C: It was found to be tissue factor
options.D: It was found to be calcium
options.E: It was found to be fibrinogen

questions.explanation: Factor VI does not exist; it was found to be activated factor V. B: It was Va. C: That is factor III. D: That is factor IV. E: That is factor I.

questions.stem: Which clotting factor is absent from circulating blood until injury exposes it?
questions.explanation: Tissue factor (III) is not in blood; it is exposed by injury. A: Circulating substrate. C: In plasma. D: Carried by vWF in plasma. E: In plasma.

questions.stem: A septic man has oozing from line sites. Platelets are 40 × 10⁹/L, PT and aPTT are prolonged, fibrinogen 0.8 g/L, and D-dimer is high. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Low fibrinogen (normal 2–4 g/L) is seen in DIC and severe liver disease; DIC prolongs PT and aPTT, consumes platelets and raises D-dimer. A: Prolongs the PT, not the aPTT. B: Isolated aPTT; normal fibrinogen. D: Normal PT and aPTT. E: Normal PT, aPTT and fibrinogen.

questions.stem: Activated factors that escape the injury are washed downstream by flow. Which organ clears them?
questions.explanation: Flow washes activated factors downstream and the liver cleans them: one of four brakes that keep the clot at the injury. B: Not shown as the clearing organ. C: Not shown as the clearing organ. D: Not shown as the clearing organ. E: Not shown as the clearing organ.

questions.stem: A woman with inherited antithrombin deficiency has a DVT. Besides thrombin, which activated factor is poorly neutralized?
questions.explanation: Antithrombin mops up thrombin and factor Xa. A: Destroyed by protein C + S. B: Destroyed by protein C + S. C: Blocked by TFPI. E: Not a target shown.

questions.stem: A newborn with severe protein C deficiency has widespread clotting. Which activated factors escape inactivation?
questions.explanation: Protein C + protein S destroy factors Va and VIIIa. A: Antithrombin targets. B: TFPI. C: Not protein C targets. D: Antithrombin.

questions.stem: Failure of a natural brake on coagulation causes thrombosis in each of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: If one brake fails the patient clots: antithrombin, protein C or protein S deficiency, or factor V Leiden. Factor XI deficiency causes mild bleeding. A: A failed brake. B: A failed brake. D: A failed brake. E: Va resists the protein C brake.

questions.stem: Which enzyme dissolves the fibrin clot as the vessel heals?
questions.explanation: Plasminogen activators turn plasminogen into plasmin within the clot; plasmin slowly dissolves fibrin. B: Activates plasminogen. C: Makes fibrin. D: Cross-links fibrin. E: Inhibits thrombin.

questions.stem: A patient with a pulmonary embolus receives a tissue plasminogen activator. Which product rises in his blood as the clot dissolves?
questions.explanation: Plasmin dissolves fibrin into fibrin degradation (split) products; D-dimer measures fibrin breakdown. A: Not a breakdown product. B: Converted to plasmin. C: Not a breakdown product. E: Not a breakdown product.

questions.stem: A deficiency of a fibrinolysis regulator protein most likely causes which problem?
questions.explanation: Deficiency of any of the regulator proteins of clot lysis increases the risk of thrombosis. A: Factor problem. B: Platelet problem. C: Not the effect. D: Not the effect.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl has petechiae and gum bleeding that starts right after she brushes her teeth. Which part of hemostasis is most likely defective?
questions.explanation: Primary (platelet or vessel) disorders: immediate, spontaneous mucocutaneous bleeding with petechiae. Secondary (factor) disorders: delayed joint, muscle and deep tissue bleeds. A: Delayed deep bleeds. C: Tertiary hemostasis. D: Thrombosis, not bleeding. E: Not mucocutaneous bleeding.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy develops a swollen knee several hours after a fall. Small cuts stop bleeding normally. Which disorder fits best?
questions.explanation: Clotting factor problems: bleeding delayed by hours into joints, muscles and deep tissue; bleeding after small cuts usually normal. Classic example: hemophilia A and B. A: Primary pattern. B: Primary pattern. D: Vessel disorder. E: Vessel disorder.

questions.stem: A woman has heavy periods and nosebleeds. Which other finding would point to a platelet or vessel problem rather than a factor deficiency?
questions.explanation: Platelet or vessel problems: immediate bleeding from skin and mucosa, petechiae, purpura, nosebleeds, heavy periods, gum bleeding, prolonged bleeding after small cuts. A: Factor pattern. B: Factor pattern. C: Factor pattern. D: Factor pattern.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl has heavy periods, nosebleeds and a recent knee hemarthrosis. How is her bleeding pattern classified?
questions.explanation: Mixed platelet and coagulation disorders combine mucocutaneous and deep tissue bleeds (e.g., vWD). B: No joint bleeds. C: No mucocutaneous bleeds. D: Not joint bleeds. E: Not this picture.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy has profuse epistaxis. Which history item best points to an inherited bleeding disorder?
questions.explanation: History includes bleeding in the neonatal period and after dental extraction, surgery, circumcision or trauma, alongside questions for malignancy (weight loss, night sweats, fever, masses) and diet, drugs and travel. A: Malignancy. B: Malignancy. C: Infection. E: Infection or malignancy.

questions.stem: A child with epistaxis also has bruises. Which history item suggests a malignancy?
questions.explanation: Weight loss, night sweats, fever, lymphadenopathy, masses and a distended abdomen raise concern for malignancy. A: Bleeding disorder. C: Bleeding disorder. D: Factor deficiency. E: Mucocutaneous bleeding.

questions.stem: Which family history item suggests an inherited bleeding disorder?

options.A: Early heart attack in the father
options.C: Iron deficiency in a vegetarian mother
options.D: Hysterectomy at a young age in an aunt

questions.explanation: Family history: consanguinity, bleeding in parents, siblings and relatives, hysterectomy at a young age. A: Thrombosis, not bleeding. B: Hemolysis. C: Diet. E: Not relevant.

questions.stem: A boy has recurrent hemarthroses, but his family history is negative. What is the best interpretation?

options.C: An inherited disorder is still possible
options.E: A vessel disorder is most likely

questions.explanation: A negative family history does not exclude an inherited bleeding disorder. A: Not established by family history. B: A negative history does not exclude it. D: It is needed. E: Joint bleeds point to factors.

questions.stem: When examining a child with bleeding, each of the following is specifically sought EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Exam: general appearance, fever or hypothermia, skin bleeding, retinal hemorrhages, hemarthrosis and contractures, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, masses, bone deformities or absent bones. A: Sought. B: Sought. C: Sought. D: Sought.

questions.stem: A man with cirrhosis and a large spleen has a platelet count of 70 × 10⁹/L. What is the main mechanism?
questions.explanation: A low platelet count (normal 150–400 × 10⁹/L) comes from marrow failure, destruction or splenic pooling. B: Not the main mechanism here. C: Not suggested. D: Not suggested. E: Not suggested.

questions.stem: A man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation is monitored with the INR. What is the usual target?
questions.explanation: INR = PT standardized between laboratories; 0.8–1.2 untreated; used to monitor warfarin, usual target 2–3. A: Normal untreated range. C: Too low. D: Higher than the usual target. E: Too high.

questions.stem: A patient on unfractionated heparin has a normal fibrinogen level. Which test is prolonged?
questions.explanation: Thrombin time is prolonged by heparin and by low or abnormal fibrinogen; heparin also prolongs the aPTT. A: A count, not a time. B: Fibrin breakdown. D: Normal by the stem. E: Warfarin monitoring.

questions.stem: A healthy woman at 30 weeks of pregnancy has a mildly raised D-dimer and no symptoms. What is the best interpretation?

options.B: It confirms a deep vein thrombosis

questions.explanation: D-dimer measures fibrin breakdown (normal < 500 µg/L) and rises in thrombosis, DIC, pregnancy, infection and surgery. B: D-dimer is not specific. C: D-dimer is not specific. D: Measured separately. E: Not measured by D-dimer.

questions.stem: A man with a mild bleeding tendency has a prolonged aPTT and a normal PT. Which cause fits?
questions.explanation: Normal PT + prolonged aPTT (intrinsic only): hemophilia A or B, factor XI or XII deficiency, heparin, vWD, lupus anticoagulant. A: Prolongs the PT. B: Prolongs the PT. C: Normal tests. E: Prolongs both.

questions.stem: A man with early liver disease has a coagulation screen. Which result is expected first?

options.A: A prolonged aPTT with a normal PT
options.E: A prolonged PT with a normal aPTT

questions.explanation: Prolonged PT + normal aPTT (extrinsic only): factor VII deficiency, early warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency, early liver disease. A: Intrinsic pattern. B: Not the early pattern. C: Not the early pattern. D: Not the early pattern.

questions.stem: A patient bleeds. PT and aPTT are prolonged; the thrombin time and fibrinogen are normal. A single deficiency of which factor fits?
questions.explanation: Both prolonged: common pathway or several factors (liver disease, DIC, full warfarin, deficiency of X, V, II or fibrinogen). A normal thrombin time and fibrinogen leave X, V or II. A: PT only. C: aPTT only. D: Normal tests. E: Prolongs the thrombin time.

questions.stem: A girl has heavy periods and easy bruising. Her platelet count is normal, and her PT and aPTT are normal. Which diagnosis remains possible?
questions.explanation: Both normal = not a factor problem: platelet disorder, vWD, vessel wall disorder, factor XIII deficiency. B: Prolongs the aPTT. C: Prolongs the PT. D: Prolongs the PT. E: Prolongs the PT.

questions.stem: A boy's prolonged aPTT corrects after his plasma is mixed 1:1 with normal plasma. What does this show?
questions.explanation: Mixing study: mix 1:1 with normal plasma and repeat. Correction = a factor is missing; no correction = an inhibitor (an antibody). A: It would not correct. B: An inhibitor. C: An inhibitor. D: Not tested by aPTT.

questions.stem: A woman's prolonged aPTT does not correct on a 1:1 mix with normal plasma. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: If the mix does not correct, an inhibitor (an antibody) is present; if it corrects, a factor is missing. A: Would correct. B: Would correct. C: Would correct. E: Normal aPTT.

questions.stem: A man has taken warfarin for six months. Both PT and aPTT are prolonged. What is the best explanation?

options.A: A factor VIII inhibitor has developed

questions.explanation: Early warfarin lowers factor VII first (PT only); the full warfarin effect lowers several vitamin K-dependent factors (II, IX, X too), so both PT and aPTT are prolonged. A: Would not prolong the PT. B: Not suggested. D: That is DIC. E: Normal PT and aPTT.

questions.stem: A boy with severe factor VIII deficiency bleeds into a knee. In the cell-based model, which phase fails?
questions.explanation: Propagation needs the tenase complex (IXa + VIIIa) on activated platelets to make the large thrombin burst; without VIII, the burst fails. A: VIIa/TF still makes a little thrombin. C: Primary hemostasis is intact. D: Factor XIIIa. E: Fibrinolysis.

questions.stem: A woman not on heparin has a prolonged PT, aPTT and thrombin time. A single deficiency of which factor fits?
questions.explanation: Thrombin time measures fibrinogen to fibrin; it is prolonged by heparin or low or abnormal fibrinogen. Fibrinogen deficiency also prolongs PT and aPTT. B: Normal thrombin time. C: Normal thrombin time. D: Normal thrombin time. E: PT only.

questions.stem: Months after a DVT, a man's clot has not dissolved. A defect in which protein best explains this?
questions.explanation: Tissue plasminogen activators turn plasminogen into plasmin within the clot, and plasmin slowly dissolves fibrin. A: Neutralizes thrombin; does not dissolve fibrin. B: Destroys Va and VIIIa; does not dissolve fibrin. C: Cross-links fibrin. E: Stops initiation.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has mucocutaneous bleeding. His platelets lack GPIb. Which step of hemostasis fails?
questions.explanation: GPIb is the vWF receptor; platelets anchor to the endothelium through GPIb binding vWF (adhesion). A: GPIIb-IIIa. B: Endothelin. C: Endothelial injury. D: Factor XIIIa.

questions.stem: A child bleeds after a tooth extraction. His PT is prolonged and his aPTT is normal. A deficiency of which factor fits?
questions.explanation: Prolonged PT + normal aPTT (extrinsic only): factor VII deficiency, early warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency, early liver disease. A: Prolongs the aPTT. C: Prolongs the aPTT. D: Prolongs the aPTT. E: Normal PT and aPTT.
